name: ssh
description: Protects against destructive SSH operations like remote command execution and key management.

destructive_patterns.name: ssh-remote-rm-rf
destructive_patterns.description: SSH remote execution contains destructive rm -rf command.
destructive_patterns.explanation:
Executing rm -rf on a remote system via SSH can cause irreversible data loss. \ Remote systems often have different directory structures and you may not have \ the same safety mechanisms in place.

\ Safer alternatives: \ - SSH in and run commands interactively with confirmation \ - Use --dry-run or preview flags when available \ - Ensure backups exist on the remote system

destructive_patterns.name: ssh-remote-git-reset-hard
destructive_patterns.description: SSH remote execution contains destructive git reset --hard command.
destructive_patterns.explanation:
Running git reset --hard on a remote server discards all uncommitted changes. \ On production servers, this might destroy deployment state or configuration \ changes made directly on the server.

\ Safer alternatives: \ - git stash on the remote first to save changes \ - Use git status remotely to check for uncommitted work \ - Consider proper deployment pipelines instead of direct remote git

destructive_patterns.name: ssh-remote-git-clean
destructive_patterns.description: SSH remote execution contains destructive git clean -f command.
destructive_patterns.explanation:
Running git clean -f on a remote server permanently removes untracked files. \ This might delete logs, uploads, or configuration files that were never \ committed to the repository.

\ Safer alternatives: \ - Run git clean -n first to preview what would be deleted \ - Use .gitignore to protect important untracked files \ - Back up untracked files before cleaning

destructive_patterns.name: ssh-keygen-remove-host
destructive_patterns.description: ssh-keygen -R removes entries from known_hosts file.
destructive_patterns.explanation:
Removing entries from known_hosts weakens protection against man-in-the-middle \ attacks. The next connection will trust any key presented by the remote host.

\ Safer alternatives: \ - Verify the new host key fingerprint before removing old entry \ - Use ssh-keyscan to preview the new key \ - Update entry rather than removing (add new key, then remove old)

destructive_patterns.name: ssh-add-delete-all
destructive_patterns.description: ssh-add -d/-D removes identities from the SSH agent.
destructive_patterns.explanation:
Removing SSH identities from the agent will require re-authentication for \ subsequent connections. Using -D removes ALL identities, which may interrupt \ active sessions or scripts.

\ Safer alternatives: \ - Use -d to remove specific keys rather than -D for all \ - List keys with ssh-add -l before removing \ - Re-add keys immediately if needed

destructive_patterns.name: ssh-remote-sudo-rm
destructive_patterns.description: SSH remote execution with sudo rm is high-risk.
destructive_patterns.explanation:
Executing sudo rm on a remote system bypasses normal permission restrictions \ and can delete system files. Combined with SSH, there's no interactive \ confirmation and errors may not be visible.

\ Safer alternatives: \ - SSH in and run sudo commands interactively \ - Use mv to a backup location instead of rm \ - Implement proper cleanup scripts with safety checks
